en: What deception is this that has taken form —
will you accept defeat before it?
Shame, shame, shame.
You are a hero, conqueror of the world,
and this woman is woven of illusion —
will you build a cage
for this mirage?
Shame, shame, shame.
Shame, shame, alas, what shame is this —
false is my beauty, false my adornment.
This is a vain heaven of dreams,
this is only a moment's offering —
is this your gift?
Shame, shame, shame!
What god is he, and in what jest
has he set us afloat on illusion's raft?
Companions of the dream, come, let us revel
in heaven's playful game.
On streams of melody, on waves of laughter,
we shall float in sport from breeze to breeze,
in the swaying of dance,
in the honey-scent of the madhabi grove,
in hours languid, gladdened, entranced.
The flower garland you have swung today
upon the thrilling breast,
keep it fresh through the honeyed night
in the heady waters of enchantment.
At the falling rays of the newly risen sun
it will droop, alas, stricken with shame;
when day is done, in the new dawn
it will fade beneath the dust
by whose neglect?
Unrest has struck today — what burning anguish is this!
The heart is pierced by a pitiless arrow
streaming with pain.
A flame of fire blazes in the breast,
a mirage trembles before the eyes —
who has strung upon death's thread my
garland of welcome?
The familiar world was lost
in dream-shadow,
in the palash-red of spring days,
in coloured illusion.
My journey is without destination,
the intoxication of losing the way has seized me,
to an unknown land now it is my
turn to go.
Ash covers the weary fire;
will you keep us at this game, O God,
how much longer?
What must come to an end,
let it end with ease.
Let the beautiful depart, leaving a trace of the dream.
Do not let wither, do not,
what once was new.
No, no, no, friend, there is no fear, no fear —
when the flower has finished its play
it is then that fruit sets.
Let the year, unconscious with joy,
leave behind its incantation's touch —
a newer pulse of rhythm.
Alone I have passed the hours of separation
gathering flowers of the sky.
All paths came and merged at last
in your two eyes.
Even as we watched, in a new light,
what did it build in the thrill of meditation —
a new world in a new heaven
in our united eyes.
In the outer sky the clouds close in,
they came to cover all the stars.
That lost light spread its seat
only in the eyes of two.
My speechless, lonely weeping
has striven for utterance,
the ache of a whole life's word
was stilled in the eyes of us both.
Why does weariness come, bearing its load of languor,
body, mind and life worn day and night with lassitude?
Tear apart this instant this mist that blots out valour;
in this prison void of deeds, in what delusion do you linger?
Ho, here they come, they come, the robber band,
roaring down like flood waters.
Come, you men of Panchagram,
come, you men of Kalinga,
come from the wrestlers' village,
cry 'Victory to Chitrangada',
cry it, cry it, brothers —
no fear, no fear, no fear, none at all.
The bewilderment of hesitation is an insult to yourself.
Do not grow faint imagining danger.
Be free of fear,
hold strength within yourself, conquer your own self.
Protect the weak, strike down the wicked,
never know yourself as poor and helpless.
Be free of fear,
keep no doubt in leaning on yourself.
When righteousness calls with the conch's blast,
silent and humble, pledge your life.
Be free of fear,
in arduous tasks give stern proof of yourself.
Chitrangada, the princess —
what can she be like,
so I wonder in my mind.
I hear that in tenderness she is woman,
in valour she is man,
I hear that enthroned she is like
the goddess who rides the lion.
If you know, tell me, beloved,
tell me of her.
Fie, fie, she is ugly, ill-formed.
She has no such arched pair of brows,
no such bright kohl-dark pupils.
It can fix upon the target —
her bowstring-scarred arm —
but it cannot pierce a hero's breast
with the arrow of a sly sidelong glance.
No modesty, no timidity,
no cruel, beautiful play,
no silent music of gesture
eloquent with hinted rhythm.
My eagerness is restless beyond measure —
where is she, that woman of valour?
A sword-blade unsheathed —
terrible she is, beautiful she is
with the fierce mood of the lifted thunderbolt,
she is no lure for the pleasure-seeker's eyes,
she is the dread glory of a Kshatriya arm.
In woman's graceful, alluring play,
why this weariness so soon?
Is the game already over, friend?
The sweet delight that entranced you —
was it a honey-smeared delusion,
was it a gift of dream,
was it an insult to truth?
You fill your heart with far-off vain hope,
you shape an image of stern love,
with what thought do you seek in woman
the quest for manliness?
Is this too a gift of illusion?
If suddenly, by force of spell,
this pliant loveliness
our friend should all at once
tear off like another's garment
and fling it in the dust,
it will not be borne, not borne, that despair —
that roaring laughter of fate,
I know, I know, friend, will torment
the greedy heart of man,
and strike a cruel arrow.
If we should meet,
then with her
I will race away
to rescue the afflicted.
From the languor of pleasure
I will leap into the torrent of battle.
Today within my restless blood
rings a clangour, clashing, clashing.
Chitrangada, the princess,
man and woman united in one.
Fortunate is she,
that at long last her summons
has reached your hero's heart.
Today let the moonless night
come to its end.
Tomorrow, in the blessed white morning,
you shall have sight of her;
the woman veiled in falsehood
will cast off illusion's veil.
Take it, take it, take it back —
this boon of yours,
O god of love.
Give me release, dispel
this net of falsehood,
O god of love.
My stolen treasure I will give back
at your feet —
the beauty of my body;
let the red flush of my lips fade away
in the ashoka grove, O god of love.
Let it pass, let it pass, this deception,
let this dream pass, O god of love.
So be it then, so be it,
let the tinted mist disperse,
let the white light appear.
Let illusion yield the road,
let love's chariot of victory come,
the beauty beyond beauty —
may the lover's eyes behold it —
from the sight let it fall away, fall away,
the slough of delusion.
When will you appear adorned without adornment?
Why today should ornament remain a veil?
If love is mingled with illusive spell,
in light and dark we shall lose each other,
my heart comes racing at your simple call —
why then make of ornament a veil?
To one whose eyes are drowned in feeling's nectar,
what splendour can you show with jewels?
Having come near, why do you yet remain far?
Will outward bonds bind the friend?
Will you steal what is your own treasure —
why then today should ornament be a veil?
Come, come, noblest of men,
come, come, my hero.
Watching your road,
the lamp stands lit.
Today at a heroine's hands you shall wear,
on your proud brow, friend,
the hero's garland of welcome.
She will tear away
her pride of strength,
at your feet she will offer
the basket of self-surrender,
at your feet she will offer it.
Today the heroine will set upon your
proud brow, friend,
the hero's garland of welcome.
O son of Kunti,
because it pleased you,
your friend filled both your hands
with a basket of beauty,
bringing flowers plucked from the garden of paradise
with long striving.
If the worship is ended,
then give the command, Lord:
let the tray of spent offerings
lie outside the temple.
Now look with gracious eyes
upon her who serves you.
I am Chitrangada, daughter of the lord of kings.
I am no goddess, no ordinary woman.
One who would worship me and set me on high —
that I am not, not I;
one who would slight me and keep me behind —
that I am not, not I.
If you keep me at your side
in peril and in fortune,
if you give consent that in hard vows
I may be your helper,
then you shall come to know me.
Today I make only this declaration —
I am Chitrangada, daughter of the lord of kings.
Quencher of thirst, beautiful of form,
come, breaker of separation's burning grief.
Set the breast swaying,
paint upon the eyes,
with the brush of dream, the kohl of sweetness.
Bring into the heart,
into the dance of the blood,
the bees' humming of the bakul bower.
Overflowing, tumultuous,
the surge of the Yamuna,
the south wind's kiss in the trembling bamboo grove.
Bring to the new leaves
a billowing dance,
the vine's embrace around the ashoka bough.
Come, come, Spring, to the earth —
bring again and again new melody,
bring new life,
new song,
bring the languid breeze heavy with scented wine,
bring into the heart of hearts of the world
a deep awakening.
Bring a new surge of rapture,
bring, bring the swing of joy's rhythm
to the earth.
Break, break the chains of bondage,
bring, bring the ache of kindled life
to the earth.
Come to the trembling, quivering,
murmur-loud,
honey-scent-thrilled
bower of malati vines restless with flowers,
in happy shade, in honeyed breeze.
Come, blossoming and eager,
come, ever-yearning,
eternal traveller on the paths of paradise.
Bring the night of union deep with flute-song,
the brimming cup of nectar
bring with you.
Come, dawn-footed, lotus-hued,
into the lap of young daybreak.
Come in the moonlight-swooning midnight,
come to the silent bower-cottage,
to lake waters happily asleep.
Come like a lightning-flash in the storm's wild sweep,
in the rocking of ocean waves.
Come in the morning loud with waking,
come to city, meadow and forest,
come into deed, word and mind.
Come with anklets humming at your feet,
come with a sweet throat loud with song.
Come in a lovely jasmine garland,
come robed in tender young leaves.
Come, beautiful one, in the rush of youth.
Come, proud hero, in new fire.
O unconquerable, march out to victory
in the battle that defeats decay —
scattering flower-pollen on the wind,
your restless tresses streaming.
